title: Louisa May Alcott didn't want to write Little Women
hook: Alcott wrote her most loved book on request, and thought the first chapters dull.
peek: Louisa May Alcott only started Little Women because her publisher asked for a story for girls. She found the work slow going, and her editor agreed the opening was dull. Then some young readers got hold of it.
lede: By 1867 Louisa May Alcott was earning a living from stories and sketches, but she had no wish to write for girls. Thomas Niles of the Boston publisher Roberts Brothers asked her for one anyway. Her journal from 1868 records that she began Little Women and plodded on, though she did not enjoy that sort of thing and had never known many girls besides her sisters.

bullets.text: Alcott sent Niles the first twelve chapters in June 1868. Her journal says he thought them dull, and so did she. She kept going anyway, treating the book as an experiment.
Niles gave the manuscript to some girls, including a niece, and they loved it. Their verdict carried the day. The first part came out in autumn 1868, sold quickly and brought demands for a sequel.

Niles advised Alcott to keep her copyright and take royalties rather than a one-off payment. It was good advice: Little Women made her financially secure and let her support a family that had long been short of money.
Readers wrote begging her to marry Jo to Laurie. Alcott refused, writing in her journal that she would not do it to please anyone, and paired Jo with the older Professor Bhaer instead.
